chapters.title: The Council of Clouds
chapters.focus: inversion · cleft sentences · hedging · tone and attitude

pages.text: Cloud Castle was not so much built as persuaded into existence: its towers, the legend went, had been argued up out of the mist by generations of eloquent councillors. On arrival, {hero} learnt that the fifth page had been [[confiscated|officially taken away from someone]] by the council, who were now debating whether a mere visitor could be trusted with it.

q.q: What does the opening sentence suggest about Cloud Castle?
options: Its people prize persuasive argument.
It was built quickly by skilled workers.
Nobody knows who designed it.
It is slowly vanishing into the mist.
q.explain: Towers “argued up out of the mist” is a playful way of saying the castle runs on argument and persuasion.

pages.text: The chief councillor, a silver-haired heron named Lady Quillon, opened proceedings with a speech that was, on the face of it, entirely courteous. Yet beneath the compliments ran an unmistakable thread of doubt. “We are, of course, delighted to welcome our young guest,” she said, “although one might wonder why a stranger should succeed where our own scholars have so [[conspicuously|in a way that is very easy to notice]] failed.”

q.q: What is Lady Quillon's real attitude towards {hero}?
options: politely sceptical
openly hostile
genuinely delighted
quietly impressed
q.explain: Courteous on the surface (“delighted”), but “an unmistakable thread of doubt” underneath: polite scepticism.

pages.text: {hero} chose not to answer the [[jibe|a short unkind remark meant to hurt]] directly. “What matters,” {hero} replied, “is not who reads the Storybook, but whether its stories are shared. Locked in your vault, the page helps no one. Returned to the book, it helps every child who opens it.” A murmur rippled through the hall; rarely had the council heard its own logic turned so neatly against it.

q.q: Why was the council's reaction significant?
options: {hero} had beaten them at their own game.
{hero} had insulted them in public.
Visitors were seldom allowed to speak.
Nobody had read the Storybook before.
q.explain: “Rarely had the council heard its own logic turned… against it” — {hero} out-argued the arguers.

pages.text: The vote was close, but the page was returned. As {hero} left, Lady Quillon fell into step beside them. “I may have been a little [[hasty|too quick, without thinking carefully]],” she conceded, with what was almost a smile. “Should you ever wish to join the council, the door will be open.”

q.q: “Should you ever wish to join” means…
options: If you ever want to join
You ought to join soon
You should not wish to join
Whenever you were asked to join
q.explain: Inverted conditional: Should you ever wish… = If you ever wish…

final.q: The scholars “conspicuously failed”, meaning they failed…
options: in a way everyone could see
without anyone noticing
by only a tiny margin
because they gave up early

chapters.title: The Great Weather Quarrel
chapters.focus: inversion · cleft sentences · hedging · tone and attitude

pages.text: Not since the Great Drizzle of the previous century had Cloud Castle been so divided. The Festival of Kites was three days away, and the castle's two weather sprites, Nimbus and Sola, could not agree on the forecast. Nimbus wanted a gentle rain to make the gardens sparkle; Sola insisted on [[unbroken|continuous, with no stops or gaps]] sunshine. Lady Quillon, now {hero}'s firm friend, asked {hero} to help settle the matter.

q.q: What does “Not since the Great Drizzle… had Cloud Castle been so divided” suggest?
options: The castle had not argued this much in a very long time.
The Great Drizzle had caused the present quarrel.
The castle argues fiercely about the weather every single year.
The Great Drizzle happened just before the festival.
q.explain: Inversion after “Not since” stresses how rare this is: nothing like it for about a hundred years.

notes.The Great Drizzle had caused the present: The Drizzle is only a point of comparison. The quarrel is about the festival forecast.
notes.The castle argues fiercely about the wea: The opposite: the castle hadn't been this divided since “the previous century”.
notes.The Great Drizzle happened just before t: It was in “the previous century”, long before this festival.

pages.text: Both sprites presented their case at length. Sola argued that rain would spoil the kites; Nimbus argued that without rain, the famous cloud-roses would [[wilt|droop and go soft because they have no water]]. “With respect,” Sola said, in a tone that suggested very little respect indeed, “nobody flies a kite to look at roses.”

q.q: How should we read Sola's “With respect”?
options: It sounds polite but is really dismissive.
It shows Sola truly admires Nimbus.
It means Sola is about to agree.
It is an apology for interrupting Nimbus mid-sentence.
q.explain: The narrator says the tone “suggested very little respect indeed”: polite words hiding scorn.

The narrator tells us the tone showed “very little respect indeed”.
Sola goes on to mock the roses, so no agreement follows.
notes.It is an apology for interrupting Nimbus: Nobody was interrupted. It's a polite-sounding way to disagree.

pages.text: {hero} listened carefully and then asked a question nobody had [[thought of|had the idea of]]: “When exactly are the kites flown?” It was, as it turned out, only in the afternoon that the kites went up. The roses, meanwhile, were at their best in the early morning. “So perhaps,” {hero} suggested, “it might be possible to have a little rain at dawn, and sunshine after lunch?”

q.q: Why does {hero} say “perhaps… it might be possible”?
options: to make the idea sound gentle, not bossy
because {hero} is not sure rain exists
to show that the plan is already agreed
because {hero} wants the sprites to refuse
q.explain: Hedging (perhaps, might) softens a suggestion so both sides can say yes.

notes.because {hero} is not sure rain exists: {hero} isn't doubting rain. The words soften the suggestion.
notes.to show that the plan is already agreed: Nobody has agreed yet. Hedging comes before agreement, to invite it.
notes.because {hero} wants the sprites to refu: {hero} wants both sprites to accept, and the gentle wording helps.

pages.text: There was a long pause. Then Nimbus, rather [[grudgingly|without wanting to, unwillingly]], admitted that a dawn shower would suit the roses perfectly. Sola conceded that an afternoon of sunshine was all the kites had ever needed. What surprised everyone most was not the solution itself, but how simple it had been all along. On the day, the gardens sparkled at breakfast and the sky was full of kites by three o'clock.

options: how simple the answer had been
that the sprites stopped speaking
that it rained all afternoon
that the roses wilted after all
q.explain: “What surprised everyone most was… how simple it had been all along.” (a cleft sentence puts the surprise in focus)

notes.that the sprites stopped speaking: They paused, but then both sprites agreed out loud.
notes.that it rained all afternoon: The plan was rain at dawn and sun after lunch, and the sky was full of kites by three.
notes.that the roses wilted after all: The gardens “sparkled at breakfast”, so the roses were fine.

options: unwillingly, though you do it
joyfully and with great energy
quickly, without any thought
secretly, so no one notices
final.explain: Nimbus agreed grudgingly: he did it, but he didn't really want to.

notes.joyfully and with great energy: Nimbus only “admitted” it after a long pause, so not joyfully.
notes.quickly, without any thought: There was “a long pause” first, so it wasn't quick.
notes.secretly, so no one notices: Nimbus said it out loud, in front of everyone.

pages.text: Rarely had Cloud Castle looked so cheerful. Dawn rain had left the cloud-roses sparkling, just as Nimbus had hoped, and by midday Sola's unbroken sunshine stretched across the sky. Lady Quillon asked {hero} to walk the kite field before the guests arrived. “It is not the weather that worries me,” she said carefully, “so much as the guests' [[tempers|how calm or cross someone feels]].”

q.q: What does “Rarely had Cloud Castle looked so cheerful” emphasise?
options: How unusually happy it looked that day.
That the castle looks cheerful at every single festival.
That Nimbus had caused a brand-new quarrel.
That the roses had wilted after all that rain.
q.explain: Inversion after “Rarely” stresses how uncommon this cheerfulness is.

notes.That the castle looks cheerful at every: “Rarely” means this is unusual, not every festival.
notes.That Nimbus had caused a brand-new quarr: Nimbus and Sola had already agreed. The line is about the castle's mood.
notes.That the roses had wilted after all that: The roses were “sparkling”, so they hadn't wilted.

pages.text: It was the guests' nerves, not the forecast, that needed settling. Two visiting sprites arrived early and began to argue about whose kite was higher. “With the greatest respect,” one began, in a tone that suggested the opposite, “mine is clearly the finer craft.” {hero} [[cleared their throat|made a small sound to get attention politely]] and pointed at the picnic rugs. “Perhaps we might all sit down before the flying starts?”

q.q: How should we read “With the greatest respect” here?
options: Polite words hiding a cold boast.
It shows the sprite truly admires the other kite a lot.
It means the sprite is about to give the kite away.
It is an apology for arriving far too early.
q.explain: The narrator says the tone “suggested the opposite”: polite words covering a boast.

notes.It shows the sprite truly admires the ot: The tone “suggested the opposite” of respect.
notes.It means the sprite is about to give the: The sprite is boasting, not giving anything away.
notes.It is an apology for arriving far too ea: Arriving early isn't what the phrase addresses; it's a dismissive boast.

pages.text: What calmed everyone, in the end, was not a speech but a shared sandwich. Once the visiting sprites were eating, their voices softened. {hero} suggested — gently, with a string of hedges — that the kites might be flown in turns after three o'clock, so nobody's string would tangle. “It might be worth trying,” Sola murmured. Nimbus nodded, almost [[eagerly|with keen willingness]] this time.

q.q: Why does {hero} use soft hedges like “might” and “worth trying”?
options: to keep the plan sounding friendly
because {hero} doubts that any kites can fly at all
to prove the plan has already been firmly ordered
to make the sprites refuse on purpose
q.explain: Hedging keeps a suggestion gentle so proud guests can agree without losing face.

notes.because {hero} doubts that any kites can: {hero} isn't doubting flight. The soft wording invites agreement.
notes.to prove the plan has already been firml: Nothing has been ordered yet. Hedging comes before agreement.
notes.to make the sprites refuse on purpose: {hero} wants them to accept; gentle wording helps.

pages.text: At three o'clock exactly the field filled with colour. Never before had so many kites shared one patch of sky without a single tangle. What surprised Lady Quillon most was how quiet the proudest guests had become — quieter, even, than the cloud-roses in the breeze. “It would seem,” she told {hero} with a small smile, “that lunch is a more powerful [[diplomacy|the skill of keeping peace between people]] than any speech I had prepared.”

options: how quiet the proud guests became
that the heavy rain returned at three o'clock
that no kites at all were brought to the field
that Nimbus suddenly restarted the quarrel
q.explain: “What surprised Lady Quillon most was how quiet the proudest guests had become.” (cleft focus)

notes.that the heavy rain returned at three o': The plan was sunshine after lunch, and the sky filled with kites.
notes.that no kites at all were brought to the: The field “filled with colour”, so the kites were there.
notes.that Nimbus suddenly restarted the quarr: Nimbus nodded eagerly; there was no new quarrel.

options: keeping peace between people
a special kind of sandwich filling
a brightly coloured type of kite string
a loud argument about the festival weather
final.explain: Lady Quillon means keeping peace — and jokes that lunch did it better than a speech.

notes.a special kind of sandwich filling: Lunch helped, but diplomacy itself is the peace-keeping skill, not the sandwich.
notes.a loud argument about the festival weath: Diplomacy is the opposite of a loud argument.

pages.text: Seldom had Lady Quillon planned a quieter thank-you. After the kite afternoon she invited Nimbus, Sola, the visiting sprites, and {hero} to a cloud-side picnic where even the cloud-roses seemed to lean in and listen. “It is not the sandwiches that matter,” she said lightly, “so much as sitting still together.” Her tone was warm, almost [[mischievous|playfully cheeky in a kind way]].

q.q: What does “Seldom had Lady Quillon planned a quieter thank-you” emphasise?
options: How unusually peaceful this thank-you was.
That she plans loud thank-yous every single week.
That Nimbus had started another weather quarrel.
That the cloud-roses had all wilted overnight.
q.explain: Inversion after “Seldom” stresses how uncommon this quiet thank-you is.

notes.That she plans loud thank-yous every sin: “Seldom” means this quiet plan is unusual, not weekly noise.
notes.That Nimbus had started another weather: Nimbus nodded at the kites; this line is about the picnic's peace.
notes.That the cloud-roses had all wilted over: The roses “lean in and listen”, so they haven't wilted.

pages.text: What settled the last of the guests' nerves was not another speech but a shared cloudberry tart. One sprite began, “With all due admiration for yesterday's flying—” in a tone that still edged toward ranking kites. {hero} [[steered|gently guided]] the talk toward the tart's jam instead. “Perhaps we might simply enjoy the view for a minute?”

q.q: How should we read “With all due admiration…” here?
options: Polite words that still lean toward a boast.
A full apology for bringing no kite at all.
Proof the sprite wants to give the tart away.
A weather report about tomorrow's rain.
q.explain: Like “with the greatest respect” before, the tone still edges toward ranking — polite cover for pride.

notes.A full apology for bringing no kite at a: The tone “edged toward ranking kites”, not a full apology.
notes.Proof the sprite wants to give the tart: The sprite is talking about flying, not giving tarts away.
It isn't a forecast; it's boast-tinged politeness.

pages.text: Never before had the cloud parade [[drifted|moved slowly with the wind]] so slowly past one picnic rug. What {hero} suggested — softly, with a string of hedges — was that each guest might name one kind thing another guest had done, rather than whose kite had flown highest. “It might be rather nice,” Sola murmured. Nimbus agreed, almost shyly this time.

q.q: Why does {hero} hedge with “might” and “rather nice”?
options: to keep the idea sounding gentle and easy to accept
because {hero} thinks kindness games are impossible
to order the parade to stop at once
to restart the weather quarrel on purpose
q.explain: Hedging keeps a suggestion friendly so proud guests can join without losing face.

notes.because {hero} thinks kindness games are: {hero} believes it can work; soft wording invites yes.
notes.to order the parade to stop at once: Nothing is ordered. Hedging comes before agreement.
notes.to restart the weather quarrel on purpos: {hero} wants peace; the hedges invite kindness, not a quarrel.

pages.text: By the time the last cloud-float had passed, even the proudest sprite was laughing. What surprised Lady Quillon most was how little anyone mentioned winning. “It would appear,” she told {hero} with that same small smile, “that jam and turn-taking are a sturdier [[alliance|a friendly team-up between people]] than any speech I keep rewriting.”

options: how little anyone mentioned winning
that heavy rain cancelled the whole parade
that no guests came to the picnic at all
that Nimbus restarted the old quarrel mid-tart
q.explain: “What surprised Lady Quillon most was how little anyone mentioned winning.” (cleft)

notes.that heavy rain cancelled the whole para: The parade drifted past; rain didn't cancel it.
notes.that no guests came to the picnic at all: Guests were there laughing. The surprise was the lack of winning talk.
notes.that Nimbus restarted the old quarrel mi: Nimbus agreed shyly; there was no new quarrel.

final.q: An “alliance” is closest in meaning to…
options: a friendly team-up between people
a loudly ranked list of kite heights
a single cloudberry left on a plate
a storm scheduled for Friday night
final.explain: Lady Quillon means a friendly team-up — jam and turn-taking beat another speech.

notes.a loudly ranked list of kite heights: Ranking kites is the opposite of an alliance.
notes.a single cloudberry left on a plate: A tart helps, but alliance is the team-up itself.
notes.a storm scheduled for Friday night: No storm here; alliance means people joining kindly.
